headline.headline: HARDEN CLIMBS INTO HISTORY, PASSES CURRY ON ALL-TIME PLAYOFF SCORING LIST
headline.deck: A vintage step-back three lifts Harden past Curry into the top 10 postseason scorers ever.
headline.body:
James Harden has never lacked for a flair for the dramatic, and he picked his spot perfectly Friday night, burying a step-back three-pointer that vaulted him past Stephen Curry and into 10th place on the NBA's all-time postseason scoring list. The moment was vintage Harden — one dribble left, a hard lean back, the ball arcing through the net before the crowd had time to process what it had witnessed. He joins a list that includes Larry Bird, Shaquille O'Neal, and Hakeem Olajuwon, players whose careers became defined by their performances when the calendar turned to May.

Harden's rise up the list comes at a moment when the 2026 playoffs have already delivered their share of memorable performances. The guard, who has spent years accumulating postseason volume in Houston, Brooklyn, Philadelphia, and Los Angeles, now owns a piece of NBA history that no trade or controversy can take away. The milestone three gave his team a critical boost in a second-round series where every possession has carried extra weight.

For Curry, the slip to 11th is a minor footnote in a legendary career, and the Golden State star is expected to reclaim the spot before his own postseason run concludes. But Friday night belonged to Harden, a player who has weathered enormous scrutiny throughout his career and responded the only way he knows how — by putting the ball in the basket when it mattered most.

secondary.headline: RANGERS REELING: SMITH HOSPITALIZED WITH VIRAL MENINGITIS AS SEAGER SITS
secondary.deck: Texas faces a grim injury week with two key infielders sidelined and Houston looming.
secondary.body:
The Texas Rangers arrived in Houston for a three-game series opener Friday night carrying a lineup that barely resembled the one they envisioned this spring. Second baseman Josh Smith was admitted to a hospital and is expected to remain there for at least a week while being treated for viral meningitis, a serious illness that has blindsided the organization. Shortstop Corey Seager, who has been mired in a significant slump, was also out of the lineup, leaving Texas without two key contributors in the middle of the field against a division rival.

Smith's hospitalization is the more alarming development by far, as viral meningitis carries significant health implications beyond any baseball timeline. Rangers manager Bruce Bochy and the organization issued a statement expressing concern for Smith's well-being and indicated baseball was a secondary consideration. The club will need reinforcements from its depth roster as the series against the Astros continues through the weekend, a difficult test made considerably harder by a roster now stretched thin in the infield.

secondary.headline: AVALANCHE, GOLDEN KNIGHTS SET FOR WESTERN CONFERENCE FINAL SHOWDOWN
secondary.deck: Two of the West's heavyweights meet with a Stanley Cup Finals berth on the line.
secondary.body:
The Colorado Avalanche and the Vegas Golden Knights are set to collide in the Western Conference Finals, a matchup that features two of the most talented rosters the NHL's second round produced. The series arrives with significant baggage already attached to the Vegas side, as the league announced Friday it had stripped the Golden Knights of a second-round draft pick and fined coach John Tortorella $100,000 for an incident in which the team was found to have boxed out media from access. The penalty adds a sideshow to what figures to be a fiercely contested series.

Colorado enters the conference final riding the surge of Nathan MacKinnon, who has been among the most dominant players in the entire playoff field. Vegas, despite its front-office turbulence and now a front-office wallet lighter by six figures, possesses the goaltending depth and defensive structure that has made it a perennial threat in May. The series opener is expected early next week, and scouts on both sides have spent the second round preparing for what many around the league consider the de facto Western Conference championship game.

secondary.headline: FORMER NFL LINEMAN JOSH MAURO DIED FROM DRUG OVERDOSE, REPORT SAYS
secondary.deck: Toxicology results reveal the former defensive end died from a combination of fentanyl, cocaine, and ethanol.
secondary.body:
A toxicology report has confirmed that former NFL defensive lineman Josh Mauro died from an acute combination of fentanyl, cocaine, and ethanol intoxication, according to a report released Friday. Mauro, who played for several teams during his professional career including the Oakland Raiders and New York Giants, had been found dead earlier this year. The findings place his death among a growing and sobering list of professional athletes whose lives have been cut short by the fentanyl crisis ravaging communities across the country.

Mauro was 33 years old. The NFL Players Association and several former teammates expressed grief at the news, and advocacy groups pointed to his death as a reminder that the fentanyl epidemic does not spare athletes whose professional careers might suggest otherwise. No foul play has been indicated, and investigators closed their inquiry upon receiving the toxicology results. Mauro is survived by family members who have not issued a public statement.

column.headline: HARDEN BELONGS IN THE CONVERSATION NOW, WHATEVER YOU THINK OF HIM
column.body:
There has never been an easy relationship between James Harden and the sports-watching public. The complaints are well-documented — the flopping, the ball-stopping, the exits from cities that ended badly enough to curl wallpaper. But Friday night, when he rose up over a closing defender and drained the step-back three that pushed him past Stephen Curry and into the top 10 on the all-time playoff scoring list, none of that history changed the number on the board. Harden is now in the company of Hall of Famers, and the ledger demands that be acknowledged plainly.

The postseason scoring list is the hardest one to crack because it requires not just talent but longevity, opportunity, and the nerve to keep shooting when seasons are on the line. Harden has done that across franchises, through controversy, and through the kind of public scrutiny that would have driven lesser competitors into early retirement. Passing Curry is not a small thing. Curry is arguably the greatest shooter who ever lived, and his postseason scoring total reflects fifteen years of deep playoff runs. The fact that Harden reached him at all says something that even his loudest critics will eventually have to sit with.

story.headline: BLAKE SNELL SHELVED INDEFINITELY AS DODGERS ROTATION TAKES ANOTHER HIT
story.deck: Left-hander scratched from Friday start with loose bodies in pitching elbow
story.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers, already navigating the treacherous waters of a long baseball season, absorbed another significant blow Friday when left-hander Blake Snell was pulled as a late scratch from his scheduled start at Angel Stadium after doctors discovered loose bodies in his elbow. The timeline for his return remains open-ended, leaving the defending World Series champions scrambling to fill a rotation spot with no clear resolution in sight.

Snell, who signed with Los Angeles in the offseason looking to rebound after an injury-marred 2024 campaign, had made only one previous start this season before the elbow issue surfaced. Loose bodies in the elbow are fragments of bone or cartilage that can cause pain, locking and swelling, and often require surgical intervention depending on severity. The Dodgers have not yet announced whether Snell will need an operation, but an indefinite designation rarely signals good news for a pitching staff already stretched thin.

The injury drama extends beyond Chavez Ravine. In Texas, Rangers second baseman Josh Smith was hospitalized and is expected to remain under care for at least a week while being treated for viral meningitis, a serious condition that will sideline the 26-year-old indefinitely. Meanwhile, slumping shortstop Corey Seager sat out Friday's series opener against the Astros in Houston, giving the Rangers' lineup a decidedly diminished look heading into a crucial divisional matchup.

story.headline: PISTONS SUFFOCATE CAVALIERS, ROLL TO 84-70 VICTORY
story.deck: Detroit's defense smothers Cleveland, pushing the Pistons closer to a series advantage.
story.body:
CLEVELAND — The Detroit Pistons turned Rocket Mortgage FieldHouse into a house of horrors for the Cleveland Cavaliers on Friday night, grinding out a punishing 84-70 victory behind a suffocating defensive effort that held Cleveland to one of its lowest scoring outputs of the postseason. The Pistons controlled the tempo from the opening tip, refusing to allow the Cavaliers to find any rhythm in their halfcourt offense and forcing turnover after turnover in a performance that had Detroit's bench on its feet for most of the fourth quarter.

Cleveland's offense, which had been one of the more dangerous units in the Eastern Conference during the regular season, looked lost against Detroit's switching schemes and physical perimeter defense. Donovan Mitchell, the Cavaliers' primary scoring option, was hounded into a miserable shooting night, finding little daylight against a Pistons squad that treated every possession like a street fight. Detroit's big men clogged the paint, neutralizing Evan Mobley's interior game and forcing Cleveland into a steady diet of contested mid-range jumpers that rattled in and out.

The Pistons, who have drawn comparisons all postseason to the blue-collar Bad Boy teams that built this franchise's identity, executed their game plan with uncommon discipline. Detroit's offense was hardly pretty — 84 points rarely is — but it was relentless, patient and efficient enough to bury a Cavaliers squad that never found an answer. The Spurs and Timberwolves did not play Friday, leaving Detroit's victory as the night's defining statement in a playoff race growing more compelling by the hour.

story.headline: NHL STRIPS GOLDEN KNIGHTS OF PICK, FINES TORTORELLA $100K FOR MEDIA INCIDENT
story.deck: League comes down hard on Vegas just as conference finals against Colorado loom.
story.body:
The NHL dropped the hammer on the Vegas Golden Knights on Saturday, stripping the franchise of its second-round draft pick and levying a $100,000 fine against head coach John Tortorella after the team was found to have boxed out members of the media from access they are entitled to under league rules. The punishment arrives at one of the worst possible moments for Vegas, which is preparing to open its Western Conference Finals series against the Colorado Avalanche with the hockey world watching every move the organization makes.

Tortorella, the 61-year-old bench boss known for his combative relationship with reporters throughout a career that has included stops in Tampa Bay, New York, Columbus and Philadelphia, did not immediately comment on the ruling. The loss of a second-round selection is a significant blow to a Golden Knights organization that has relied on savvy drafting and aggressive trades to sustain its contending window since entering the league in 2017. General manager Kelly McCrimmon built much of Vegas's depth through mid-round picks, making this penalty sting beyond the optics.

The timing casts a shadow over what should be a marquee Western Conference matchup. The Avalanche, led by Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar, enter the series as a dangerous opponent capable of exploiting any distraction inside the Golden Knights locker room. Vegas still boasts Jonathan Marchessault, Mark Stone and goaltender Adin Hill, but the front office now carries the weight of a league sanction into one of the most important series the franchise has played since hoisting the Stanley Cup in 2023.

story.headline: QUARTERBACK CAROUSEL SPINNING FAST AS NFL TEAMS RESHAPE ROSTERS THIS SPRING
story.deck: Several franchises are making bold moves at the most important position in football.
story.body:
The NFL offseason is producing seismic shifts at quarterback, with multiple franchises committing massive resources to signal-callers in what league observers are calling one of the most active springs in recent memory. The Cleveland Browns agreed to terms with veteran quarterback Sam Darnold on a three-year, $132 million contract, betting the former Pro Bowler can finally provide the stability the franchise has chased for decades. Meanwhile, the Las Vegas Raiders moved aggressively in the trade market, sending two first-round picks to the Tennessee Titans in exchange for Will Levis, whose cannon arm and mobility fit new offensive coordinator Brian Callahan's scheme perfectly.

The 2026 NFL Draft, held last month in Washington D.C., offered little relief to teams still searching for franchise quarterbacks, as the class was considered thin at the top. The New York Giants used the fourth overall pick on Colorado wide receiver Travis Hunter, pivoting away from a quarterback selection after failing to land a trade partner willing to move up. Draft analysts praised the Jacksonville Jaguars for selecting Texas offensive tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. in the first round, giving Trevor Lawrence a cornerstone to build around for years.

Training camps remain two months away, but roster construction is already defining which teams project as legitimate contenders heading into the 2026 season. The Kansas City Chiefs quietly bolstered their defensive front by signing edge rusher Haason Reddick away from the New York Jets, while the Philadelphia Eagles retained most of their Super Bowl LX championship core through shrewd contract restructuring. General manager Howie Roseman extended tight end Dallas Goedert and cornerback Quinyon Mitchell within the same week, signaling the Eagles intend to defend their title with the same nucleus that delivered Philadelphia its latest Lombardi Trophy.
